extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, critics and writers interested in P. G. Wodehouse's life and comic-writing techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of P. G. Wodehouse's techniques for composing comic fiction and prose, including plotting, language devices, character handling, and tonal choices that produce humour. Useful for writers and critics studying or attempting a Wodehouse-like comic style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough plotting and scenario planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Before starting a book Wodehouse would write up to four hundred pages of notes ... He always completed the plot before working on specific character actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare extensive notes and a complete plot before writing scenes; Wodehouse often produced a fuller scenario (~30,000 words) to avoid plot holes. Planning may take a long time (even years) and multiple novels can be prepared in parallel. Ensure the plot is fully worked out so the placement of comic situations is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-focused structuring to locate comedic moments
rubrics_metrics.description: For a humorous novel you've got to have a scenario, and you've got to test it so that you know where the comedy comes in ... splitting it up into scenes (you can make a scene of almost anything) and have as little stuff in between as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the scenario into discrete scenes and 'test' the scenario to identify where comedy arises; make scenes the primary unit of comedic action and minimise irrelevant filler between scenes so comic beats remain sharp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meticulous drafting and multiple revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wodehouse would ensure that his first draft was as carefully and accurately done as possible, correcting and refining the prose as he wrote, and would then make another good copy, before proofreading again and then making a final copy for his publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the first draft with precision; revise in successive clean copies with proofreading at each stage. Emphasise clarity and polish in each pass rather than relying on a single rough draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplined writing routine and steady output
rubrics_metrics.description: He preferred working between 4 and 7 pm—but never after dinner—and would work seven days a week. In his younger years, he would write around two to three thousand words a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a consistent daily routine and disciplined hours to sustain high output and momentum; established routines help produce large volumes of comedic prose reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a lighthearted, escapist tonal worldview
rubrics_metrics.description: Wodehouse believed that one of the factors that made his stories humorous was his view of life: 'If you take life fairly easily, then you take a humorous view of things.' He described the approach as 'making the thing a sort of musical comedy without music, and ignoring real life altogether.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a tone that treats events lightly and avoids heavy realism; favour an upbeat, unserious outlook that lets humour arise from trivial disasters and genteel absurdity rather than moral or political weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an idyllic, self-contained setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of Wodehouse's canon is set in an undated period around the 1920s and 1930s ... The critic Anthony Lejeune describes the settings ... as 'a fairyland'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a largely unchanging, timeless or slightly anachronistic world (an 'artificial world' or 'fairyland') that isolates comic characters and situations from modernity and real-world pressures; consistency of setting supports recurring jokes and character types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat characters as actors and keep them actively employed
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with the dialogue in his novels, Wodehouse would consider the book's characters as if they were actors in a play, ensuring that the main roles were kept suitably employed throughout the storyline, which must be strong: 'If they aren't in interesting situations, characters can't be major characters...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plots so principal characters are repeatedly placed in interesting, scene-worthy situations; avoid characters who exist only to be talked about—action and situational engagement define character prominence and comic opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stereotypes deliberately but reveal human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of Wodehouse's parts were stereotypes ... yet within the stereotypes Wodehouse understood human nature, and therefore 'shares with [Charles] Dickens and Charles Chaplin the ability to present the comic resistance of the individual against those superior forces...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ recognisable, stock character types to speed audience recognition, but give them believable human traits or resistances that allow for comedic conflict and sympathy; stereotype alone should be offset by insight or nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive word-formation and playful neologisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques used include the creation of new words through adding or removing prefixes and suffixes ... Wodehouse created new words by splitting others in two (e.g., 'de-Beaned the cupboard'; splitting 'hobnobbing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate morphology (prefixes/suffixes), split words, and coin playful neologisms to produce surprise and comic effect. Use such devices to characterise voice and to produce light lexical humour without confusing the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate use and subversion of clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Voorhees believes that the author used clichés in a deliberate and ironic manner ... Medcalf deems Wodehouse's skill is to 'bring a cliché just enough to life to kill it' ... Pamela March considers Wodehouse to have 'an ability to decliché a cliché'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce familiar clichés and then tweak, subvert, or over-animate them so that recognition turns into comic deflation. Using clichés ironically can both reassure and surprise readers when the cliché is 'killed' by fresh phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative imagery and incongruous similes
rubrics_metrics.description: The stylistic device most commonly found in Wodehouse's work is his use of comparative imagery that includes similes ... humour comes from Wodehouse's ability to accentuate 'resemblances which at first glance seem highly incongruous'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create similes and comparisons that pair disparate domains (e.g., distant sheep coughing / pigs feeding in a thunderstorm) to produce a comic cognitive jolt. Repeat such imagery sparingly to maintain the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparing use of transferred epithets for comic colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Hall also identifies that periodically Wodehouse used the stylistic device of a transferred epithet ... The form of expression is used sparingly by Wodehouse in comparison with other mechanisms, only once or twice in a story or novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply transferred epithets (adjectives that grammatically modify one noun but logically relate to another) occasionally to add whimsical nuance; avoid overuse so the device retains its freshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay including puns, linguistic confusion and mixed metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordplay is a key element ... puns (e.g., 'a pinched look'), linguistic confusion ('assaulted by the duck pond'), mixed metaphors and exaggeration are frequently used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a variety of verbal tricks—puns, deliberate ambiguity, equivocation, mixed metaphors and hyperbolic comparisons—to create multiple layers of laugh-worthy meanings. Use them in service of characterisation and scene, not merely as ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-specific malapropisms and imperfect vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Bertie Wooster's half-forgotten vocabulary also provides a further humorous device ... example exchange around 'cataclysms'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give characters distinctive, fallible ways with words (half-remembered vocabulary, malapropisms, near-misses) to create personality and recurring comic beats; ensure such quirks are consistent and reveal character rather than obscure meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of period slang and literary/allusive texture
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of Wodehouse's use of slang terms reflects the influence of his time at school ... Another favoured source was the King James Bible and many poets are quoted or alluded to throughout his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sprinkle period-appropriate slang and literary allusions to give texture and voice, but balance these with accessibility so readers grasp the humour. Allusions and biblical phrasing can be repurposed for comic contrast when juxtaposed with trivial situations.
